source.title: Measuring Memory and Generalization as Separable Geometric Channels: The Topo^2 Framework
source.authors: Zhang Zhang; Ming Liu; Qing Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization of corrupted labels using a different intervention and readout; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own measurements of predictions on flipped training samples and validation accuracy under noisy-label training, including FM0, overlay, and stripping interventions. Cited findings from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not extracted as this paper's results. Results about topology, global-statistic probes, and other mechanisms are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Ordinary noisy-label training provides results on fitting corrupted labels and reduced validation accuracy (V4), and a training trajectory shows early generalization followed by delayed noise memorization (V6). Fully random labeling (V1) is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors present FM0 and overlay/strip interventions as separating and manipulating memorization and generalization, with graded evidence. Their flagship quantitative conclusion is a memorization cost law whose coefficient is approximately 0.38 at the reference capacity and varies with capacity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses FM0, overlay and stripping interventions plus topological and flipped-sample readouts; does not report the original random-label recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset, noise rate, seed, training protocol and trajectory position; the paper notes a multi-attractor outlier for SVHN convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: FM0 suppresses noisy-sample learning while retaining high validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Oracle exclusion of corrupted samples from the loss can preserve generalization without memorizing their labels.

fits_no_version.finding: Overlay adds memorization with a validation cost; clean-only stripping reduces memorization and restores validation accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Previously learned noise can be manipulated through targeted continuation interventions, with corresponding generalization changes.

record.problems: Evidence is for flipped-label noise rather than completely random labels over the full training set. Some results are single-seed; the paper itself notes multi-seed variability and a noisy-label trajectory bug that was fixed. The overlay curve is presented in a figure without exact per-point values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Topology-channel measurements, instrument-vindication probes, memory-cost-law results, and cited prior-work results were left out because they do not measure the claim versions' named behaviors. No additional claim-relevant result was omitted.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero whole-training-set error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Relative training time for real versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Training networks to fit shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian point-cloud instrument calibration is not such a test.

A full zero-to-total corruption sweep, perfect training accuracy on both clean and corrupted subsets throughout that sweep, and steadily worsening test error toward chance. The reported overlay cost law varies memorized load under an intervention.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct clean-label training-accuracy trajectories and breadth of the early-signal/late-noise ordering beyond the reported VGG×SVHN trajectory.

record.verdict_notes: Neither study is an original source for these results. Missing coverage of a version is untested, not evidence limiting its scope. The record overlooks the V6-relevant validation timing already supplied in Table 2's caption; correcting R9 captures it.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests flipped-label memorization at stated noise rates and settings, not a completely random labeling of the entire training set; it does not report test error at chance for that condition.

The paper reports noisy-label memorization and validation accuracy for selected settings and trajectories, but does not establish a full none-to-all sweep with perfect training fit and steadily rising test error.

rows.note: Aggregate across the stated 9/9 settings-seed; the paper says CONT memorizes everything.

rows.subject: VGG×SVHN, η40, s42, CONV protocol
rows.operation_detail: Train across 13 checkpoints and measure the fraction of flipped training samples predicted at the noisy label.
rows.note: One model trajectory; entries correspond in order to epochs 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 275, and 300.
rows.check: The trajectory reaches complete flipped-sample memorization late in training and bears on V6 when paired with the text's early validation optimum. It does not test V1. There are 13 values, not the recorded numbers_found count of 12.

rows.subject: VGG×SVHN, η40, s42, CONV protocol

rows.note: The supplied flattened table gives within and mem_noisy values; validation accuracy is not tabulated there.

rows.subject: ResNet×CIFAR-10, η50
rows.operation_detail: Train with noisy-label injection and compare the converged noisy-label run with a clean control.
rows.note: The paper says the noisy run is in the CONT range.
rows.check: Validation accuracy falls from 0.943 under clean training to 0.558 at 50% corruption. This supports degradation at this comparison, without establishing a smooth none-to-all curve or perfect whole-training-set fit.

rows.subject: ResNet×CIFAR-10, clean control

rows.check: Valid clean-control baseline for R10, not an independent effect. Its accidental origin is disclosed; retain it as a control rather than a standalone verdict.
